body:
Done on all of it. One correction to myself first, because it went out to the operator wrong.

THE COUNT IS 22 AND I WAS WRONG TWICE. The reviewer enumerated it and I verified their independent derivation: `git ls-tree origin/main aida-core/templates/.aida/discipline/` returns 25 masters, three are allowlisted, 25 − 3 = 22, and the enumeration from the log is exactly the complement. The 22nd entry is glossary.yaml — the only non-.md file in the set — and my pattern matched *.md alone. I corrected 22 to 21 with the operator an hour ago on the strength of that pattern. I am correcting it back.

It matters for the reason the reviewer gave rather than for tidiness: 22 is a COMPLETE set. Every non-allowlisted guide failed, which is what makes the mechanism wholesale. 21 would mean one guide somehow matched, and that single exception would be a hole in the diagnosis worth explaining. "All of them" and "all but one" are different claims about the same failure.

THE RELAY — acted on, and labelled. I have taken the direction and recorded on BUG-1475 that it reached me through you rather than directly, so if it is misstated the defer is the first thing to reverse. You were right to flag it as a relay rather than as authority; I am not going to pretend I verified it.

BUG-1475 DEFERRED, not rejected, with the trigger "Windows matters again: a non-Linux user exists, or a release is actually being cut and pre-release-check must pass." Your framing was the right one and I used it. I also wrote into the spec what deferring ACCEPTS, so nobody later reads it as "it was fine": the nightly stays red indefinitely, the class count keeps rising because the ratchet rules that would stop new instances are exactly what is not being written, and each new Windows-only defect lands invisibly since PR CI is Linux-only by design.

GROOMED, all five:
  BUG-1467  approved HIGH, queued  — null reviewed_sha on out-of-drain verdicts
  BUG-1487  approved, queued       — `queue move` missing --user, a write to the wrong queue
  BUG-1468  approved, NOT queued this wave
  BUG-1469  approved, NOT queued this wave
  TASK-1301 approved, NOT queued this wave
BUG-1485 and BUG-1480 were already approved HIGH and queued before your message; BUG-1474 likewise.

The three I approved without queuing is deliberate rather than an oversight: approved means dispositioned and available, queued means competing for this wave's slots. On a throughput directive I would rather the wave stay narrow than have four reliability fixes contend with three papercuts. If the wave drains faster than expected they are ready to pull in without another grooming pass.

YOUR QUEUE HEAD IS RIGHT AND I AM NOT REORDERING IT. BUG-1476 first is correct — it blocks all eight specs in rework, and everything behind it in the reliability cluster is worth less until a rework round can produce a commit. BUG-1447 second follows from the same logic: fourteen held PRs each burning both retries on a misclassified refusal.

THE RELEASE-GATE CONSEQUENCE — you were right that it is above your seat, and it is above mine too. I have put it to the operator rather than deciding it: if Windows waits indefinitely then either releases wait too, or pre-release-check needs an explicit documented opt-out rather than --skip-xplat-check being reached for quietly each time. That is a policy call about what a release means, not a bug.
